summary: A 1979 request for comments on ideas for naming, addressing and delivery in ARPANET message systems. It is not a specification of a protocol about to be implemented but a set of concepts for the next generation of mail systems.

eli5.summary: This asks for thoughts on how to name people and deliver their mail in the future. It is a brainstorm.

subtitle: A brainstorm on the future of computer mail: names, addresses, and delivery systems.

tldr.problem: The current ARPANET message system conflates names (who you are) with addresses (where you are), making it hard to change hosts or use human-readable names in mail.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 757 proposes separating identity from location using unique user IDs that persist across moves, with a distributed network database that maps IDs to delivery addresses. Local mini-databases can cache commonly used entries.
tldr.outcome: This is a brainstorm requesting feedback on future mail systems, not a specification for immediate implementation.

today: This RFC is a historical brainstorm on mail system design. Modern email addresses (SMTP) eventually adopted a hierarchical namespace through DNS. Later proposals like X.500 and LDAP explored directory services for email lookup, but DNS and SMTP became the dominant standard.

sections.title: Problems With Today's Mail System
sections.content: The ARPANET message system evolved from informal beginnings and lacks a clean separation between a person's identity and their address. Users must know the exact mailbox location (hostname), and when a person changes hosts, their name and address both change. The system also forces users to employ machine-friendly designations like user@host instead of human names. Additionally, mail delivery extends the File Transfer Protocol, which is limited to simple point-to-point transfers and cannot bundle multiple messages or fan-out messages at the destination.
sections.eli5: When you move to a new office, your mail address changes, and everyone has to update their records. This is a mess.

sections.title: A Network Identity and Address Database
sections.content:
RFC 757 proposes assigning each authorized user a unique, persistent network ID that never changes, even when they move between hosts or networks. A distributed network database would map each ID to one or more delivery addresses, with delivery priority if multiple addresses exist. Users could be identified by their human name, initials, or other information in this database, freeing mail composition programs from requiring exact addresses.

Rather than centralizing the database (which would create bottlenecks), RFC 757 suggests a distributed approach where each host maintains local mini-databases of commonly used IDs and addresses. When a local entry is not found, the host queries the network database and caches the result for future use.
sections.eli5: Everyone gets a permanent, unique ID. Your address can change, but the ID stays. Mail servers keep local notes of people they talk to, asking a shared directory only for new people.

sections.title: Delivery and Local Processing
sections.content:
The delivery process consists of three parts: determining the address from the recipient's ID (consulting local or network databases), sending the message to that address, and having the receiving host process it. Unlike the current system which delivers mail to a single user, the proposed system allows bulk mail to multiple recipients with the same message, bundled mail sending multiple messages in one connection, and combinations of both.

The receiving host could perform various processing functions in a local mail room: sorting bundled or bulk mail, performing fan-out to multiple users, re-broadcasting to the network, or other services chosen by the host administrator. This flexibility allows different message processing styles while maintaining a common delivery standard.
sections.eli5: The post office can now deliver one letter to many people at once, or group many letters going to one person. The destination host can sort them however it wants.
